conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting, just a way to see how your mood and anxiety are doing so we can best support you. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll go at your pace in a safe, judgment-free space. When you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things lately?
I’ve laughed a little—maybe once or twice when my husband made a joke—but mostly I don’t really feel the urge. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wouldn’t say that. I mean, I’ve managed a small chuckle here and there, but it’s not the same as before—I have to force it, and the joy doesn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Sometimes I do—like when my sister said she’d come over for coffee—but it’s pretty half-hearted. Mostly I’m just going through the motions; the excitement I used to feel isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I start thinking it’s because I’m not doing something right, or that a “better mom” would know how to fix it. It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit. Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing—even when he’s right next to me and fine. It passes pretty fast once I check on him, but it keeps happening out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of “what if something’s wrong?” It’s usually when he’s sleeping really still and I have to watch his chest rise. It’s a rush of nerves for a minute, then I’m okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel like I’m barely treading water. I still get everything done—mostly—but it feels heavier than it should, like I’m constantly a step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, sleeping itself isn’t the problem. I drift off okay once the baby’s down; it’s just that some nights my mind keeps ticking through the next day’s tasks or little worries about him, so it takes an extra half-hour or so.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it comes and goes. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel this wave of sadness, like I’m missing something I can’t name. It’s not every hour, but most days there’s at least a stretch where I just feel kind of down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when I dropped a plate and it shattered. It wasn’t really about the plate; I just felt overwhelmed and the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired or stressed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 10-item EPDS responses

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (reduced laughter, limited anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Mild–moderate dysphoria (daily waves of sadness, episodic crying)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“not a good-enough mom”) occurring several times/week  
- Discrete anxious arousal: sudden, intrusive “what-if” fears about infant safety; resolves quickly with reassurance  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “a step behind,” especially when routine tasks accumulate  
- Mild initial insomnia (30-min sleep-onset delay related to rumination)

Positive findings  
- EPDS items 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 endorsed above threshold; items 7 and 5 sub-threshold; item 10 negative.  
- No suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts reported.

Risk relevance  
- Persistent low mood with anhedonia and tearfulness raises concern for postpartum depression (mild–moderate range).  
- Recurrent, unprovoked infant-focused worries suggest comorbid postpartum anxiety features.  
- Functional impact described (“feels heavier,” “barely treading water”) without overt impairment in basic infant care.

Safety  
- Denies self-harm; no further safety red flags identified on screening.

Screening summary  
Patient exhibits several clinically significant depressive and anxiety symptoms in the early postpartum period; scores indicate need for follow-up assessment, psychoeducation, and consideration of formal evaluation for postpartum depression/anxiety.
